chunks: And from him, from al-Nadhr, from 'Asim, from Muhammad ibn Qays, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:

Amir al-Mu'minin (peace be upon him) ruled for a woman who freed a man and stipulated his 'wala' (manumission bond) for herself, and she had a son, that his 'wala' be attached to her 'asabah' (agnates) who pay his blood-money, rather than her son.

key_terms.أَمِيرُ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ: Commander of the Faithful, a title referring to Imam Ali (peace be upon him), though here used for Imam al-Sadiq in the context of the ruling.
key_terms.عَصَبَاتِهَا: Her agnatic relatives (male relatives on the father's side) who are liable for paying the blood-money (diyah) of the freed slave.
key_terms.وَلَاء: The bond of manumission, referring to the right of the manumitter to inherit from the freed slave and the obligation of the freed slave to support the manumitter.
key_terms.يَعْقِلُونَ عَنْهُ: Those who pay his blood-money; a technical term in Islamic inheritance law indicating the group responsible for diyah.

ai.seo_question: Who inherits the wala of a freed slave when the owner is a woman with a son?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights a specific juristic dispute regarding the priority of 'wala' (manumission bond) between a female patron and her agnatic kin. Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) ruled that the 'wala' attaches to the 'asabah' (male relatives liable for blood-money) rather than the son, prioritizing the financial liability structure over direct lineage in this context. This reflects the Shia emphasis on the economic and social responsibilities embedded in the institution of manumission.
